name: Acai
short: Outbreaks of acute, potentially fatal Chagas disease in the Brazilian Amazon were linked to parasite-contaminated acai juice or pulp. Adulteration of a marketed acai product was reported.
text: Outbreaks of acute Chagas disease, an infection with the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, have been linked to drinking acai juice or eating acai pulp contaminated with infected insect faeces, mainly in the Brazilian Amazon; in 2006, cohort and case-control studies in one area of the state of Para implicated acai consumption in oral transmission, and a review describes orally acquired infections as acute and potentially fatal. This is a risk from contamination of the juice or pulp rather than a property of the fruit itself, and the cited abstracts do not say whether processed supplements carry it. A review of acai and other fruit supplements sold in the United States concluded they may generally be considered safe, but noted cases of adulteration found in a commercial acai product. A systematic review of rodent studies, which gave acai mostly by mouth, found no genotoxic effects; these are animal data. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
